title: Myrtle Beach with teens and tweens
summary: Things to do when mini golf alone will not cut it
description: Ideas for visiting Myrtle Beach with teenagers and tweens: thrill rides, go-karts, escape rooms, water sports, trampolines and ways to give older kids some independence.
intro: Older kids are the hardest group to plan for. They are too big for the toddler stuff and sometimes too cool for the family stuff, but they still like to be active and to have a say. The Grand Strand has plenty for them, and the trick is to mix a few high-energy activities with space to relax.

A few notes first. Age and height minimums vary by attraction and can change, so check each place's page before you set your heart on something. Teens who are close to a minimum can be disappointed at the gate.

p: Family Kingdom Amusement Park, right on the oceanfront, has a wooden coaster and a mix of other rides, with a separate water park section. It is a good mix of old-fashioned seaside park and modern thrills. Broadway Grand Prix and K1 Speed both offer go-karts, and K1 Speed runs electric karts on an indoor track, which makes it a good option on a hot or rainy day. Check the height and age rules for each track.

Myrtle Waves is a large water park with slides and a wave pool, and it is open seasonally. For something different, try a watersports outfit such as Aloha Watersports, which offers things like jet skis, parasailing and boat-based activities, depending on the season and the operator. Surfing and paddleboarding lessons are also available from various local companies. Always ask about weather policies and minimum ages.

Escape rooms work for the age group because they involve puzzles, competition and a clock. Escapology is a good starting point. Big Air Trampoline Park is a way to burn off energy indoors. Axe throwing and other newer activities appear on our family and indoor page, with age limits that vary.

The Myrtle Beach SkyWheel is a tall observation wheel on the oceanfront, and it is popular for evening photos. It is a calm ride, and some teens enjoy it more at night with the lights. The Boardwalk around it is a natural place for older kids to wander in a group, if you are comfortable with that. Agree on a meeting spot and a time before they go.

Teens like having a little room. On busy stretches such as the Boardwalk, many parents let older kids explore in pairs or small groups during daylight, with phones charged and a clear meeting time. Choose places that fit your family's comfort level. In the evening, stay together, because crowds and traffic are heavier.

list: Morning: beach, bodyboarding or a watersports session while the sun is not too hot.
Afternoon: a big-ticket activity such as the water park, go-karts or a trampoline park, then rest.
Evening: Boardwalk, SkyWheel and a short round of mini golf, with a competitive scoring system.
Book escape rooms and cruises ahead. Teens do not enjoy waiting.
Sun protection matters more than they will admit. Pack it and require it.
Check height, age and waiver rules, since many activities require a parent or guardian to sign.
Build in downtime. A full schedule leads to grumpiness, even in older kids.
